faq.q1: How far ahead should I order?
faq.a1: Two days for most cakes, and seven days for two or three tiers. Fondant and edible photo finishes add time on top of that — the notice we need is listed on this page and it updates whenever we change it.
faq.q2: What does a cake for 60 people cost?
faq.a2: A full sheet serves 60 to 80 and starts at the price listed in the size table above. The final total depends on tiers, filling and decoration, and we confirm it with you before taking any deposit.
faq.q3: Can I bring a photo of what I want?
faq.a3: Yes. Bring a photo, or a ribbon or swatch from the dress. Our decorators work from what you bring.
faq.q4: How much is the deposit, and can I cancel?
faq.a4: The deposit and cancellation terms are listed on this page, above. We confirm the full total with you before the deposit is taken.
faq.q5: Do you make gluten-free or dairy-free cakes?

ourStory.title: Our story
ourStory.p1: When Argentina Ortega bought a 600 square foot bakery from a distant relative three years ago, she started out with four clients in a fast growing Hispanic business community.
ourStory.p2: She baked sweet Central American, South American, Puerto Rican and Mexican pastries in the morning and then distributed them wholesale to businesses in Richmond.
ourStory.p3: Today, her business supplies baked goods to about 250 Hispanic stores in Virginia, the Eastern Shore and Elizabeth City, N.C. and employs 11 people.
ourStory.p4: “We're busting at the seams right now,” the Salvadoran native said. “We don’t want to spend another winter here because that’s when business peaks, a bigger location is right on the horizon.”
ourStory.p5: They moved the bakery to a 5,000 square-foot location on 7730 Midlothian Turnpike next to the state police headquarters.
ourStory.p6: The two sons Eduardo and Mario Dawson had a construction company for seven years, but decided to invest in their mother's expanding business because of the downturn in construction. “We want to invest our money in a more stable and tranquil job for the future,” said the two sons.
ourStory.p7: The current location was a step up from Ortega's home kitchen where she began baking the pastries and selling them. But it meant more expenses and not necessarily more clients. “It was a rough start,” she said.
ourStory.p8: “I was happy if I sold $750 a week,” she said. “Now I make a lot more.”
ourStory.p9: The bakery has targeted Hispanic businesses since it opened in the early 90's. But Ortega and her sons want to go beyond the Hispanic market. “It will be a multicultural store,” said Jenny Dawson, Ortega's daughter-in-law.
ourStory.p10: The plan is to have a cafe with internet access, typical sweet Latin American pastries such as quesadillas or cheese pastries, conchas, guava filled bread and pudding. And for those looking for something more familiar, there will be muffins and other goodies for a wider clientele.
